mcqs.question: For a one-hot true label, why do all terms except the true class's term vanish in the cross-entropy loss formula -Σ y_i * log(p_i)?
options: Because y_i is 0 for every class except the true one, so those terms multiply to zero regardless of the predicted probability
Because log(p_i) equals zero for incorrect classes by definition
Because the model always predicts exactly 0 probability for incorrect classes
The terms don't actually vanish; this is a common simplification error
mcqs.explanation: With a one-hot encoded true label, y_i = 1 only for the correct class and 0 for all others, so every other term in the sum is multiplied by 0 and vanishes regardless of what probability the model assigned there. This leaves cross-entropy loss as simply -log(p_correct), the negative log of the predicted probability for the true class.

mcqs.question: A feature has near-zero linear correlation with the label but has a clear U-shaped relationship to it (e.g. very low or very high values both predict the positive class). Which selection method would correctly flag this feature as informative?
options: Pearson correlation, since it captures all forms of statistical dependence
Mutual information, since it captures nonlinear dependence, not just linear correlation
Neither method can detect a U-shaped relationship
Only a full trained model can ever detect this kind of pattern
mcqs.explanation: Pearson correlation specifically measures linear association and can be near zero even when a strong nonlinear (e.g. U-shaped) relationship exists. Mutual information measures general statistical dependence — linear or not — so it correctly identifies the feature as informative in this case, without needing to train a full model just to discover the pattern.

mcqs.question: During training, cross-entropy loss on the validation set gets worse over an epoch, but validation accuracy stays exactly the same. What's a plausible explanation?
options: This is impossible; loss and accuracy always move together
There must be a bug in the loss computation

The model may be making its already-correct top predictions no less accurate, but is becoming more confidently wrong on the examples it misses, which cross-entropy penalizes but accuracy doesn't measure
Accuracy is simply a rounding of cross-entropy, so they must always match
mcqs.explanation: Accuracy only checks whether the top predicted class is correct, ignoring confidence; cross-entropy penalizes miscalibrated confidence directly. A model can keep the same set of correct/incorrect top predictions (unchanged accuracy) while becoming more confidently wrong on its misses, which drives cross-entropy up with no accuracy change — a real, non-buggy divergence between the two metrics.

mcqs.question: Why can't a model trained with label smoothing ever drive cross-entropy loss all the way to zero, even with perfect training data?
options: Label smoothing adds random noise to the input features, capping accuracy
Label smoothing changes the model architecture to remove the final layer's ability to output confident probabilities
Zero loss would require the model's predicted probability for every class to be exactly 0, which is mathematically impossible under any smoothing scheme
The smoothed target itself is never exactly 1 for the true class, so matching it exactly still leaves a nonzero cross-entropy against the true one-hot label
mcqs.explanation: Label smoothing replaces the one-hot target (say [0,1,0]) with a softened target like [0.03,0.94,0.03]; training pushes predictions toward this smoothed target rather than the hard one. Since the smoothed target caps the true class's value below 1, cross-entropy against it can approach a nonzero floor but never reach the zero that a hard target would allow. It changes nothing about the architecture or the inputs — it only changes what the loss is computed against.
